1.pericope_label: Joshua old and stricken; ye have seen all that the LORD did

schools.summary: Weigh the place of the assembly rather than asserting one. Timnath-serah has the argument that Joshua was too old to travel, but it does not appear he took so much state upon him; Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, is likelier, and probably at one of the three great feasts when the men had come up to worship anyway. Then say why the interval mattered, since the text gives no figure: long enough for Israel to feel the comfort of their rest and enjoy the good land, and long enough for Joshua to observe which way their danger lay, namely their intimacy with the Canaanites who remained. Explain also why he addressed the rulers and not the whole people -- they could not all come within hearing, and these men would carry the substance of it into their own countries, so that the charge was dispersed through the nation; and if the great men could be prevailed on to cleave to God, their influence would keep the common people faithful. Last, make his age do double work: it was his reason for speaking now, since he could expect to be but a little while with them, and their reason for listening, since days should speak and he had grown old in their service.

Notice that the phrase about age repeats one used of Joshua years earlier, and consider the two ways of taking the sentence -- either that a long time had passed and Joshua had grown old, or that we have here the two evenings of his life, the early one when his sun began to decline and the late one just before its setting, Israel having received their inheritance between them. Set this address against the one that follows at Shechem: the first suits men of education, authority and position, and concerns the duty of rulers, while the second carries one plain lesson for all the people and makes no demand upon their intellect. Record the setting exactly: after the division of the land Joshua had withdrawn to his own inheritance to spend his last days quietly, and it was the remembrance of the charge once laid on him that drew him out to gather the people in the persons of their representatives. And read the geography as the Hebrew gives it, the starting point named in one clause and the limit in the other without its preposition, each clause completed from the other by the parallelism. Note finally what the text concedes: the conquest was preliminary and partial, Joshua having given Israel the land and the vantage-ground from which to possess it.

Date the occasion as closely as the evidence allows: the last and hundred and tenth year of Joshua's life, some thirteen or fourteen years after the conquest and seven after the division of the land. Name the four ranks summoned and what each did -- the elders or senate who were princes of the tribes, the heads of families, the judges who interpreted and decided by the law, and the officers who executed their decisions. Insist that the two great assemblies of these closing chapters are distinct meetings, whatever the place of either. Then catch the tone of the speech. Israel would naturally have credited their veteran general with the conquest, saying that without such a commander they had never gained the land; Joshua corrects the opinion and insists the battle was the Lord's and not his, which shows as much modesty as piety. Explain why the Canaanites survived at all -- not through their own bravery, their armies having long been broken, but through the supineness of Israel. And note the single Hebrew word that serves for both halves of the promise: they shall disinherit them from their sight, and shall inherit their land.

Hold two things together that seem to pull apart. The peace Israel enjoyed among the nations of Canaan is rightly described as an excellent blessing of God; and yet it was owing to their own cowardice that they dwelt among enemies whom it would not have been difficult to rout and destroy. Give God the thanks for pardoning that ingratitude, and do not soften either half. Then set Joshua's solicitude before all who hold authority as a pattern. A father is not thought sufficiently provident if he cares for his children only to the end of his own life and extends his care no further; so magistrates and rulers ought to provide that the well-ordered condition in which they leave affairs be confirmed and prolonged long after them, as the apostle undertook that the Church should remember his admonitions after his departure. And keep the smaller matters plain: the summons was occasional rather than a stated convocation, so all Israel here means the representatives, and the promise that the remainder would yet be expelled still stands over the nations that were left.

debates.question: Where and when was this assembly held?

sides.position: Probably Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, and likely at one of the three great feasts; Timnath-serah suits his age but he did not take so much state upon him
Shiloh, since words uttered before the Lord were likely to have the more effect
Undecided between Timnath-serah, Shechem and Shiloh; but this was an occasional convocation of representatives, not a stated one
The place is uncertain, but this meeting and the one at Shechem are two distinct assemblies; the date is the last and hundred and tenth year of Joshua's life
Joshua had withdrawn to Timnath-serah to enjoy his inheritance quietly, and was drawn out by the remembrance of the charge once laid on him

debates.question: Why were any Canaanites left in the land?

sides.position: By design. The preliminary and partial nature of the conquest is distinctly recognised; Joshua gave Israel the land and the vantage-ground from which to possess it, and now bids them continue the work
Through the supineness of the Israelites, the Canaanite armies having long been broken so that they could make no head against them

Through their cowardice, since it would not have been difficult to rout and destroy them; the peace they enjoyed is nonetheless an excellent blessing, and thanks are due for the pardon of their ingratitude

outliers.note: Alone offers the figure of the two evenings of Joshua's life, the early one when his sun began to decline and the late one just before its setting, observing that Israel received their inheritance between them; and alone contrasts this address, suited to men of authority, with the plainer one at Shechem that makes no demand upon the intellect.

Alone sets Joshua's forethought before all who hold authority as a pattern, arguing that as a father is not provident who cares for his children only to the end of his own life, so rulers ought to provide that the order in which they leave affairs be prolonged long after them.

6.pericope_label: Be very courageous to keep the law; cleave unto the LORD your God

schools.summary: Say what the courage is for, and do not spiritualise it away: great resolution was needed to execute all the commands of Moses, and particularly to expel the residue of the Canaanites; turning aside to the right hand or the left means adding to the law or diminishing from it. But say too that it takes no small courage to keep a sound creed among scoffers, and no less to maintain a godly practice among the profane, and that God's people are bound by his word alone, nothing being received as an article of faith which God has not spoken. On the ban against naming their gods, show the descent step by step, since that is the whole point of it: civil contracts lead to spiritual affinities, mention breeds discourse, discourse brings approbation, and approbation ends in worship -- so that things not evil in themselves are forbidden as introductions to evil, no man reaching the worst by a single step. Add the complaint that the names of the heathen gods are still commonly used among Christians, especially in poems, and let names set up in rivalry with God be loathed and lost. On the promise that one shall chase a thousand, refuse both errors: do not sit still waiting to grow numerous, and do not impute past victories to your own valour. And warn that watchfulness is harder now than in the wilderness, the temptations being stronger from bad neighbours and from prosperity itself, with the pride and forgetfulness of God that attend it.

Classify the prohibition instead of merely repeating it. To mention the names of the idols, to swear by them, to serve them with sacrifices and to bow down to them in prayer are the four outward forms of divine worship, and the verb rendered come among them means to enter into close intimacy with a person. Read the closing clause carefully: as ye have done unto this day gives a reason for persevering in the attachment they had shown, and does not affirm that they had hitherto done all these things fully and perfectly. Trace each promise back to its source in Deuteronomy, both the driving out of great and strong nations and the assurance that no man should stand before them. Then say what the law-keeping charge implies about office: Joshua was himself the servant of the law, and his successors must be the same, since no higher position is attainable and nothing can ever supersede the authority of the written word. Note also why the nations were not delivered up all at once -- the Lord reserved to himself the ordering of the conquest, and meanwhile it was a trial of Israel's faith to live among idolaters without making peace with them or lending countenance to their worship.

Guard against the counterfeit of confidence. The mode of conquering is not to indulge gross security in place of genuine trust; however confidently hypocrites contemn God, they would wish him bound to them, and often boast of his promises with no small pomposity, whereas true faith, while it reclines upon God, keeps those who possess it in his fear. Explain the strong word accordingly: to be very courageous denotes serious study, because in the great weakness of our nature no man will set about the thorough observance of the Law unless he exerts himself above his strength. On the idolatry, observe what the text does not specify -- neither bending of the knee nor sacrifices nor any particular rite -- and infer from that silence that God is defrauded of his honour whenever any particle, however small, of what he claims for himself is transferred to idols. Then define cleaving in both directions, outwardly by close adherence to his word and worship, inwardly by strong affection, trust, expectation and fixed dependence. And put the promise on its true footing: so long as they do not themselves change there will be no change on God's part, for from love to God all true obedience springs, and without free and ardent affection we study in vain to frame our lives by the external form of the Law.

Turn the charge into two rules a hearer can act on. First, always stand upon your guard, for many a precious soul is lost and ruined through carelessness; God has given us precious souls with the charge to keep them with all diligence, above all keepings, that the inward man be kept clean from the pollutions of sin and closely employed in his service. Second, let what we do in religion proceed from a principle of love, not by constraint nor from a slavish fear of God, but of choice and with delight -- love the Lord your God, and you will not leave him. Note that the word rendered yourselves is properly your souls, and let the charge fall there.

debates.question: What is the courage commanded here for?

sides.position: For the practical work: executing all the commands of Moses, and particularly expelling the residue of the Canaanites
For holding a sound creed among scoffers and a godly practice among the profane
For serious study of the Law, since in the weakness of our nature no man will set about its thorough observance unless he exerts himself above his strength
For the office itself: Joshua was the servant of the law and his successors must be, nothing superseding the authority of the written word

debates.question: Why is even naming their gods forbidden?

sides.position: Because mention breeds discourse, and discourse by insensible steps brings approbation and then worship, so that things not evil in themselves are forbidden as introductions to evil
Because civil contracts lead to spiritual affinities and so to mention, swearing, service and bowing; no man reaches the worst by a single step
Because naming, swearing, serving and bowing are the four outward forms of divine worship
Because no particular rite is specified, so all perverse worship is designated at once, and God is defrauded whenever any particle of what he claims is transferred to an idol

debates.question: Does one man chasing a thousand look backward or forward?

sides.position: Two Jewish expositors take the future for the past, recording what had already happened in the war; a third refers it forward to what they would do if they clave to the Lord, as afterwards in Samson
Forward, as a spur against inaction: they need not wait to become more numerous before driving out their enemies
Backward, as a caution: they must not impute the victories to their own valour, as they would be apt to do

outliers.note: Alone carries the prohibition into his own day, complaining that among Christians the names of the heathen gods are still so commonly used, especially in poems, and wishing that names set up in rivalry with God be for ever loathed and lost.
Alone infers from the absence of any specified rite that God is defrauded of his honour whenever any particle, however small, of what he claims for himself is transferred to idols.

themes: Be ye therefore very courageous to keep and to do all that is written in the book of the law of Moses
cleave unto the LORD your God, as ye have done unto this day
One man of you shall chase a thousand: for the LORD your God, he it is that fighteth for you

12.pericope_label: Snares and traps and thorns; not one thing hath failed

schools.summary: Open with the soldier's case, since it fixes the stake: one who draws back on going to meet the enemy forfeits his life, and these were the Lord's soldiers, so drawing back was drawing back unto perdition. Then take the four figures one at a time, because each says something different -- a net set by the fowler for heedless birds, a trap laid on the ground to catch the unwary traveller by the foot, a goad continually in the side, a thorn in the eye. Make the application plain: the surviving nations would drive Israel into the service of false gods and put out the eyes of their understanding, and God would preserve them for that very purpose. Show also what the end would feel like, that they would be forced to quit their own land and wander they knew not where, terrible to men comparing their present ease and plenty with the hazards and wants of their former wandering. State the symmetry at the centre of the argument: God's faithfulness in fulfilling his promises is the proof that he will as faithfully accomplish his threatenings, since his veracity is equally pledged for both. And where an inherited doctrine will not stand with the text, say so -- if the good land was freely and surely granted, the misery of those who perish from it cannot be aggravated by a grant they never had any share in.

Explain why threatening follows promise at all. It is the usual method of the Law: those not sufficiently allured by the divine goodness are to be aroused by fear to the performance of their duty. It is disgraceful that men do not run forward at once when God graciously condescends to invite them; but such is the lethargy of the flesh that it always requires to be stimulated by threats. Note that the warning about scourges and thorns is not made once only, and give the reason -- God had consecrated the land to himself and wished it purged of all impurities, and seeing how prone the people were to be corrupted by bad example, he provided a remedy for that evil beforehand. On the announcement of Joshua's death, read it as consolation rather than as a claim on their attention: his loss would leave the people as a mutilated trunk deprived of its head, so he tells them not to ask that his condition differ from the whole human race. Then qualify it, since the qualification matters: the form of dying is not the same in all, for those who receive the heavenly doctrine are distinguished by an incorruptible seed, and only what is common to all men is in view here. And take death itself plainly as a journey to one's long home, a path trodden by every man and but once, from which none is exempted, be he ever so great or good or useful.

Take the declaration that nothing had failed as evidence about how the promises were understood. Though the conquest was in one way a limited conquest, this statement shows that it fully satisfied the hopes of Israel for the time -- that is, they took the divine promises in the sense in which we can see them to have been actually fulfilled. Then identify the audience by the subject matter, since the exhortations concern things that lie within the province of a ruler: marriages, treaties and public worship are all under the control of law, the law must be forgotten if the magistrates will not enforce it, and what the rulers will not tolerate the people will find it hard to maintain. Supply the covenantal frame for the threat by naming its source -- the evil word is the curse of rejection already spoken through Moses in the law, and the closing verse closely resembles an exhortation in Deuteronomy. And render the strong phrase exactly: to know in all the heart and all the soul is to be fully convinced.

debates.question: What force have the four figures of snare, trap, scourge and thorn?

sides.position: Each is distinct -- a fowler's net for heedless birds, a trap for the unwary traveller's foot, a goad in the side and a thorn in the eye; the nations would drive Israel to false gods and put out the eyes of their understanding, God preserving them for that purpose
They describe a sequence: converse draws Israel by degrees into their errors, and once weakened they are molested until forced to quit the land and wander again
They are repeated deliberately, because God had consecrated the land to himself and provided beforehand against a people prone to be corrupted by bad example

debates.question: How should Joshua's announcement of his own death be read?

sides.position: As a claim on their attention, so that they would take these for his dying words; death being a journey to one's long home, trodden by all men and but once, from which none is exempted
As consolation, to prevent immoderate grief when they should be left as a mutilated trunk deprived of its head; with the qualification that the form of dying is not the same in all
As the settled conviction of men who knew in all their hearts and souls that no good word of God had failed

outliers.note: Alone quotes an earlier English expositor approvingly on how the goodness of the heavenly Canaan aggravates the misery of those shut out from it, and then turns that very sentence into an argument against the doctrine of absolute decrees, asking how a man not elected might have been happy, or an elected man wretched for ever.

Alone identifies the audience from the subject matter, observing that marriages, treaties and public worship lie within the province of the ruler, that the law must be forgotten if the magistrates will not enforce it, and that what the rulers will not tolerate the people will find it hard to maintain.

this day I am going the way of all the earth
